We just discussed this here in Toronto. The approach we settled on is:

  • bind will go, maybe to be restored later in the form of a macro
  • Function types will fall into three categories, @fn, ~fn (both boxed), and plain fn, with the latter only being allowed as a function argument that's passed by alias.
  • fn values are noncopyable. Thus, you never have a raw fn value on your hand. Boxes of functions are copyable.
  • There will be @fn(args...){body...} and ~fn(){} expressions to create boxed function values. They will close over their environment by copying the closed-over values into their environment.
  • Functions passed by alias to another function can be written as plain fn(...){...} expressions. These 'fully' close over their environment (the resulting alias holds the frame pointer). These must never outlive the function call they are passed to.
  • Function boxes can transparently be passed to a function that expects a function alias. (Or maybe require an explicit dereference with * if that causes ambiguities.)
  • As a form of syntactic sugar, a function that takes a function alias as its last argument can be called like f(args) { block }, causing the given block to become a function. If this function needs to take arguments, it becomes f(args) { |arg1, arg2| ...} (this syntax is not set in stone).
  • Function values take the form of a single-word code pointer followed by an environment (of any size). @fn and ~fn create a box of the right size and copy in the code pointer and closed-over values. Stack-allocated functions that are passed by alias have their code pointer plus a frame pointer allocated on-stack, and the address of the code pointer passed.

The issue of returning/breaking out of blocks has not been addressed yet, I'll try to bring that up later.
What is the status of named nested functions? Do those capture? Do you write things like "@fn foo(...) -> ... {...}"?

We didn't discuss in depth, but off-the-cuff, Graydon, Dave, and I agree that they probably shouldn't. That's slightly un-obvious but has the advantage of giving these function boxes a definite lifetime. If you need the equivalent of a closing local function, just assign a `~fn' to a local variable. Sounds sane?

Also, I forgot to mention, taking the name of a normally defined function with ~ or @ in front of it should result in a function box being created for that function. They can also be passed by alias. How type specialization of taking the value of a type-parametric function works wasn't discussed, but I guess we'll want to generate a specialized version of it (as bind currently does) and use that as the function value.

I understand the reasoning, but it seems inelegant to give lambdas and explicitly named functions fundamentally different semantics.

My proposal is that a nested function declared as "fn foo(args) -> t { body }" does not capture but one declared as "@fn foo(args) -> t {body }" does.

I think function boxing of normally defined functions already exists?

So, my plan for implementing this involves adding a field to fn_decl saying what form of environment capture the function does (no capture, copying capture, alias capture).

Does anybody have any thoughts on what the right way to detect what sort of capture a function needs? Can/should it be done at parse time?
Definitely don't do it at parse time. A pass that gathers free variables and puts them in a table is probably the best approach. Various stages of compilation need this information.

You misunderstand my question. Finding the free variables certainly shouldn't be done at parse time. I mean, figuring out which "flavor" of capture a function has (because the current plan seems to be to have three: no capture, copying capture, aliasing capture). Which it is depends on what context the lambda occurs in (if it is being put in a box it should capture the environment by copying it; if it is being passed by as a function argument then it's by alias). So I'm wondering when the best time to decide on that is.

Ah, I see what you mean now. I'm actually coming around to having local 'item' functions capture. You'll have to leave something in blocks or regular fn expressions to disambiguate during parsing, yes.
Capturing by default or only with an @ glyph in front or something?
Capturing by copying in the case of @fn and ~fn, capturing by storing the frame pointer in other cases.
So there wouldn't be a "don't capture at all" mode, even for item functions?
I can't make the final decision on that. Try implementing it like that, we can see how well it works.

the thing is, fn types are to be non movable (nor copyable) so you can only ever really pass a "bare" function as an alias-mode parameter. how you get one ... yeah, it'll have to be an item (inner or otherwise) or a lambda-block.

I don't see a lot of harm in permitting such inner items to capture the frame, the same way a lambda-block will.

I don't see a lot of harm in permitting such inner items to capture the frame, the same way a lambda-block will.

That's pretty much what my original write up says too.

the thing is, fn types are to be non movable (nor copyable) so you can only ever really pass a "bare" function as an alias-mode parameter.

OK. As it stands now, you can pass bare function types as non alias parameters and it works right.
(Because they do not close yet.)

Also, with regard to capturing the environment by passing the frame pointer:

For each loops are currently not done like that. For each loops are built by constructing an environment with pointers to all of the local upvars and then packaging that as the function's environment. Is LLVM smart enough to magic that into just passing a frame pointer. If not, is there a way to explicitly tell LLVM to just pass a frame pointer? Does the LLVM IR know about things like frame pointers?

Also, passing frame pointers doesn't directly extend to multiple nested lambdas. Pass multiple frame pointers in that case?

(Because they do not close yet.)

You can pass functions created with bind too, though, which do have an environment...

Function types will fall into three categories, @fn, ~fn (both boxed), and plain fn, with the latter only being allowed as a function argument that's passed by alias.

In 7476a39 I checked in the beginnings of a different approach. What I would like to do is produce a low-level Rust API that closely mirrors the C uv API, with similar performance characteristics, with minimal runtime C++ code. So the user starts an event loop which calls event handler functions, just like uv.

To do so I propose going through the libuv test suite and duplicating each test case in Rust until we have a complete implementation. At that point we can write some networking libraries. I think this is a good approach because writing these bindings is going to be a major test of both our task system and FFI so we need rock solid tests.

Pretty early you run into the issue of dealing with native callbacks, and resolving it is going to require some significant changes to the runtime scheduling code.

This is what I propose:

  • Separate rust_scheduler into rust_domain and rust_sched_thread. rust_domain is 'the scheduler' and rust_sched_thread manages the per-thread resources like the C stack and context switching.
  • Instead of the kernel having a fixed set of schedulers, it now has a dynamic set of domains which each have a fixed number of threads.
  • Implement std::task::spawn_domain which creates a new domain with some specified number of threads (in the future this can be refined with other types of domain).
  • Calling uv::run spawns 2 single-threaded domains: an event loop and an event handler, then waits for the event loop to exit. The event loop will spend all its time blocked in C code so must be in its own domain and the handler will need to respond very quickly to events so shouldn't have to deal with other tasks being scheduled ahead of it.
  • The event loop handles the native events and synchronously dispatches them to the event handler task which then presents them to the user as a Rust callback. There are several options for how to implement this and I think over time there will be opportunities to optimize, with the ultimate optimization being a mechanism to actually call Rust code from C code, eliminating the event handler task.
  • We define all of our uv handles with one extra field: rustfn, a pointer to a Rust function. When the user registers a callback, we put that callback in rustfn and register our own native function to handle the dispatch back to Rust code.

It gets more vague from here as I've only scratched the surface of the libuv API, but I believe this lays out a promising path.

I'm still open to somebody else implementing it as I don't expect to get back to libuv until sometime after 0.1.

Currently Trans.trans_call takes an argument indicating whether it's an
initializing call, but it always behaves as though it's initializing, even if
the argument is false. This is because there's a bit of a subtlety involved in
refcounted values: the same referent may be used as both dst of the call and as
an arg, and we want to avoid having it drop before being pinned as an arg,
because the dst was dropped.

The existing code may have been born in the CoW era and may no longer represent
a real hazard if rearranged to just pin args first then drop dst; will need a
few careful tests to be sure the arrangement actually works.

(Alternatively: worst case, make a static pass that prohibits x = f(x) the same
way f(x,x) is to be prohibited if both slots are alias-mode.)

A type can carry its own set of constraints. Example:

type ordered_pair = (int,int) : lt(*._0, *._1);

Implicitly, after every initialization of a slot s of type ordered_pair, there
should be a "check lt(s._0, s._1);", and after every copy statement there
should be a "prove lt(s._0, s._1)" statement, so that the implied constraints
become enforced at initialization time and preserved during writes.

This doesn't literally require adding statements -- though that's one approach
-- but it needs to mimic the effect one way or another. Currently such
constraints are simply ignored.
Shifted to rustc.

I think we actually don't want to synthesize checks here. It's more consistent IMO to require explicit check and prove statements.

We should never, in general, coerce T to T : pred. They're disjoint types.
I agree with Patrick here. I'll implement it this way unless someone yells.
How do you initialize an ordered_pair by that logic? initialize one without the constraint, check it, then move?

I'm assuming like:

check lt(a, b);
let p : ordered_pair = (a, b);

where if I omitted the check, the code would fail with a typestate error. Data constructors just get treated like functions, which can also have preconditions...
(a, b) isn't a pred. what's check doing there?
Sorry, edited.
Hm. Ok. If you can make it work, that seems sensible.
Also see: #869

I'd like to have a concise form.

How about inserting checks for explicit casts?

let p = (a, b) as ordered_pair;

See https://github.com/graydon/rust/wiki/Constrained-types for our current thinking on this (mistakes are solely due to me). A problem with inserting checks for explicit casts is that it still requires further type system restrictions. Like, suppose you wrote:

let p = (a, b) as ordered_pair;
let q : ordered_pair = p;
q = (2, 1);

This is a bad program, because (2, 1) is not of type ordered_pair. But it's not clear how to design the typechecker and typestate so as to reject it. One simple solution is just to disallow ordered_pair as a type on the LHS of a declaration.

So since we have to introduce this restriction anyway, it seems to make sense to limit the introduction forms for things that have constrained types -- that is, the only place where the name of a constrained type can appear in a declaration is a function signature.

This is still very much of an open question, so I'm open to debate. I haven't had breakfast yet, so let me know if any of this doesn't make sense ;-)

Copying from one slot to another should add a copy of every constraint that
includes the RHS of the assignment to the copy postcondition (with the RHS
renamed, in the constraint, to the new LHS slot).

In other words:

let int x = 10;
let int y = 11;
check lt(x,y); // postcond = { lt(x,y) }
let int z = x; // postcond = { lt(x,y), lt(z,y) }

Unless some horrible complications arise that make this impossible, I believe
the current rules permit this propagation to work.

Phase 2b RCA update (2026-04-25): The bug pattern reported here ('LLVM SH4 tail-call-opt drops arg-setup across extern "C"') is not a tail-call-opt issue. Phase 2b SDAG capture identified the root cause as our own SuperHFixupCallClobber.cpp post-PEI peephole pass.

The pass walks backwards from each JSR @rN looking for a MOV32PCR that defined $rN and, if it sees an intervening def of $rN (a 'clobber'), inserts a fresh $r1 = MOV32PCR <CPI> before the JSR and rewrites the JSR target to $r1. The flaw: it doesn't bail on intervening kills of $rN. If an unrelated MOV32PCR loaded a static-global address into $rN, that address was used+killed by an immediate consumer (e.g., another MOV32mr), and $rN was later reused as a legitimate JSR-target carrier (e.g., $r0 = MOV32mrd $r14, 0 for a stack-spilled fn-ptr), the pass mis-identifies the unrelated MOV32PCR as the JSR's source and rewrites the JSR target to load the unrelated global address.

In the relibc_start_v1 main() call site this manifested as: $r5 silently aliased to *(&environ) (CSE-collapse against the prior environ load) and JSR @r1 jumping to literal &argv (.bss).

Fix: bail when the backward walk sees a killed $CallReg USE — the kill flag marks the last use of the value held in CallReg from its previous def; any earlier MOV32PCR was meant for that consumer, not for the JSR. Lands in rustx-sh4 v4.4.63. Phase 2b artifacts: /var/tmp/sh4-issue18-phase2/. Arbiter contract #44.

with a 'detach x' statement, that must hold before sending; or could simply be
part of the operator definition (that it detaches any memory before sending,
along with dropping the sent slot).

Note that there may be multiply-references leaves within a value that require
detachment themselves, so detachment is a recursive predicate / operation.
